parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by a field of force.

markscheme_points.text: where a particle experiences a force

hints: Hint 1: Think about what is special about the space around a mass or a charge, even when nothing else is there yet.
Hint 2: A complete definition needs two ideas - where the effect exists, and what happens if you place a suitable test object there.
parts.proper_answer: A field of force is a region of space where a particle experiences a force.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a Field Means**
Imagine a mass or a charge sitting alone in space. It changes the space around it so that another object placed there would feel a push or pull without touching. That altered region is what we call a field.

Step 2: **Building the Two-Part Definition**
You need to say it is a region of space, and then say the test for it: a mass in a gravitational field feels gravitational force, a charge in an electric field feels electric force. Together: $$ \text{field} = \text{region where a particle experiences a force} $$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: State one similarity and one difference between the electric field due to a point charge and the gravitational field due to a point mass.

markscheme_points.text: similarity – any one point from: • both have an inverse square variation • both decrease with distance • both are radial
difference – any one point from: • gravitational field always towards (the mass) • electric field can be towards or away from (the charge)

hints: Hint 1: Compare the shapes of the two force laws, $F \propto 1/r^2$ for gravity and for electrostatics, and think about the direction of the field lines.
Hint 2: Remember mass only comes in one type but charge comes in two types, positive and negative, so think about whether the force can ever push outward.
parts.proper_answer: Similarity: both fields obey an inverse-square law with distance, both decrease with distance and both are radial. Difference: gravitational field is always directed towards the mass (always attractive), while electric field can be directed towards or away from the charge (attractive or repulsive).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Seeing the Similarity**
For a point mass, $$ g = \frac{GM}{r^2} $$ and for a point charge, $$ E = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} $$ Both have $1/r^2$ dependence. Both spread out radially from the centre and get weaker with distance in exactly the same mathematical way.

Step 2: **Seeing the Difference**
Gravity only pulls. There is no negative mass, so $g$ always points in towards the mass. Charge can be positive or negative, so $E$ points away from a positive charge and towards a negative charge. Electric force can attract or repel, gravitational force can only attract.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
An isolated solid metal sphere of radius $0.15\text{m}$ is situated in a vacuum, as illustrated in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1

The electric field strength at the surface of the sphere is $84\text{V m}^{-1}$.

Determine:
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the surface point - how far is it from the centre of the sphere, and what value of $E$ is given there?
Hint 2: Outside a charged metal sphere the charge acts as if concentrated at the centre, so rearrange the point-charge field relation to make $Q$ the subject before substituting values.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Modelling the Sphere as a Point Charge**
Outside a solid metal sphere all the charge sits on the surface, but the field is the same as a point charge $Q$ at the centre. At the surface $x = 0.15\text{ m}$ and $E = 84\text{ V m}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Rearranging and Substituting**
The governing law is: $$ E = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x^2} $$ Rearrange for $Q$: $$ Q = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 E x^2 $$ Put in $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F m}^{-1}$: $$ Q = 4\pi \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 84 \times (0.15)^2 $$ $$ Q = 2.1 \times 10^{-10}\text{ C} $$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: the electric field strength at point P, a distance $x = 0.45\text{m}$ from the centre of the sphere.
hints: Hint 1: Point P is three times farther from the centre than the surface was, so think about how strongly an inverse-square field drops with distance.
Hint 2: Use the ratio of distances squared to scale the known surface field down, or substitute $Q$ and the new $x$ directly into the field equation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Using Inverse-Square Scaling**
$E$ is proportional to $1/x^2$. Going from $0.15\text{ m}$ to $0.45\text{ m}$ is a factor of 3 in distance, so the field falls by a factor of $3^2 = 9$.

Step 2: **Calculating the New Field**
Either scale directly: $$ E_P = 84 \times \left(\frac{0.15}{0.45}\right)^2 $$ or use $Q$ again: $$ E_P = \frac{2.1 \times 10^{-10}}{4\pi \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times (0.45)^2} $$ Both give: $$ E_P = 9.3\text{ V m}^{-1} $$

parts.label: (c)

markscheme_points.text: smooth curve with decreasing negative gradient throughout, from $x = 0.15 \text{ m}$

hints: Hint 1: Think about where free charges sit in a solid metal sphere in equilibrium and what that means for the field at points with $x$ less than the radius.
Hint 2: Identify your two fixed points for the outside region - the value at the surface $x = 0.15\text{ m}$ and the value you just found at $x = 0.45\text{ m}$.
Hint 3: Recall the shape of a $1/x^2$ curve starting high and flattening out, with a steep drop at first that gets gentler.
parts.proper_answer: E = 0 for $0 \le x < 0.15\text{ m}$, then $E = 84\text{ V m}^{-1}$ at $x = 0.15\text{ m}$ falling as $1/x^2$ to $9.3\text{ V m}^{-1}$ at $x = 0.45\text{ m}$ with smooth curve of decreasing negative gradient.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Field Inside the Metal**
Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium there is no net field. All excess charge repels to the outer surface. So from $x = 0$ to $x = 0.15\text{ m}$ draw a line along $E = 0$.

Step 2: **Jump at the Surface**
At $x = 0.15\text{ m}$ the field jumps to its maximum value $84\text{ V m}^{-1}$. This is the starting point of the outside curve.

Step 3: **Inverse-Square Fall Outside**
For $x > 0.15\text{ m}$ draw a smooth curve falling as $1/x^2$ with a decreasing negative gradient, getting flatter with distance. It must pass through $(0.45, 9.3)$ in $\text{V m}^{-1}$ and $\text{m}$. No sharp kinks, just a continuous $1/x^2$ decay.
